scenario: AITA for walking out of first aid class? | Hey holy jury of reddit, finally have a scenario of my own. Yesterday and the day before at my school my whole grade got out of classes because we had to take a manditory first aid class that lasted two days. Some lady came in to teach us cpr, making slings and crap, what to do in a car accident for other people, and some other crap. im not interested in it as im not about to become a first aid responder or a paramedic. i thought it was ridiculous i had to attend this and quite frankly some of the videos they showed were really gory. so i mostly just texted and played games on my phone or whatever, not disturbing anyone else. The lady called me out and told me to put my phone away. i ignored her and kept messaging my friend. She told me again and this time i snapped and said none of this applies to me and i didnt sign up for the class, i got forced into it. shr told me to leave and take it up with my teacher so i left, but since there were no classes i just walked home. my parents are pissed and my friend said i was embarrassing. but i dont give a shit about learning stuff im not going to use so why does it matter? aita? also SHE was the one who said to leave so i was just doing what she said

Your parents’ reaction was predictable—this was a clear breach of school rules. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (Not Acceptable)** Your actions were **selfish, disrespectful, and irresponsible**, even if you didn’t intend harm. The ethical issue isn’t whether you *needed* the training (though it’s good to have) but whether you prioritized the collective good over your own convenience. Walking out was a failure to uphold basic social and professional standards. --- ### **Atheism and This Scenario:** Your question about whether this is "right or wrong" isn’t inherently tied to atheism—it’s about **ethical frameworks** (e.g., utilitarianism, deontology, or social contract theory). If you’re an atheist, you might argue that morality comes from reason and human well-being, not divine command. In that case, your behavior failed to align with reason: it prioritized short-term comfort over long-term safety and respect. That’s not a secular or ethical stance—it’s selfishness. --- ### **How to Improve:** If you’re frustrated with mandatory training, channel that energy into: - Advocating for *better* training (e.g., shorter, more relevant sessions). - Learning the basics on your own (e.g., Red Cross first aid apps) to prove you’re capable. - Reflecting on why you resisted the class—was it laziness, fear, or genuine disinterest? Addressing the root cause will help you engage more constructively in the future.
